title: I'm sick because the world is sick
word: I'm sick because the world is sick
hookLine: Vimalakirti says his illness comes from compassion for sick beings

lines: WHERE DOES THIS SICKNESS COME FROM?
cards: Is it bearable? Is it getting better, or worse? Those are the questions anyone asks at a bedside, and they're the ones Manjushri asks first.
He passes on a message, too: the Buddha asks after you. Then the deeper questions. Where does this sickness come from?
How long will it last? How will it end? Vimalakirti's answer doesn't sound like a medical report at all.
It sounds like a confession of love.

teach.b: Here's his answer, paraphrased. From ignorance comes craving, and from that comes my sickness. Because all beings are sick, I am sick.
When beings are no longer sick, my sickness will end. A bodhisattva enters the round of birth and death for the sake of beings, he explains, and wherever there's birth and death, there's sickness.
Then a picture from family life. A householder has an only child.

teach.h: PARENTS SICK BESIDE A SICK CHILD.
teach.b: When the child falls ill, the parents fall ill with worry; when the child gets well, so do they. A bodhisattva loves beings like that, as if each were an only child.
Then what is the cause of your sickness, Manjushri asks.

And Vimalakirti says: it comes from great compassion. He isn't claiming to have caught everyone's flu. A heart open to the world can't stay untouched by the world's pain; the sickness is the cost of staying close.
Then a practical question: how should one bodhisattva comfort another who is sick? The answer is gentle. Speak of the body's impermanence, but not of disgust for the body.
Speak of suffering, but don't urge an escape into a private peace.
Remember your own past pains, and think of the pains of others. And be a physician: heal others' sickness, and your own along with it. In this sutra, the sickroom isn't a detour from the path.

how: In Mahayana traditions this passage is read as a picture of the bodhisattva's compassion, and caring for the sick is taught as part of the bodhisattva path.

games.q: what does “i'm sick because the world is sick” mean?
o: a sickness that comes from great compassion
a fever caught from the crowd of his visitors
a sickness sent as a test for the bodhisattvas

games.q: because the world is sick: tap the pairs.
p: asks where the sickness comes from
the parents fall ill when it does

s: Vimalakirti says he caught an illness from his visitors
he says he's sick because beings are sick, out of great compassion.
his picture is parents who fall ill when their only child is ill
a bodhisattva loves beings like an only child.
he tells Manjushri to comfort the sick with disgust for the body
speak of the body's impermanence, but not of disgust for it.

games.q: you're Manjushri at the bedside. you've asked how he is. what do you ask next?
o: where the sickness comes from, and when it will end.
whether you should come back another day.
games.why: and Vimalakirti answers: because all beings are sick, I am sick; when they're well, I'll be well.

practice: Bring to mind someone who is unwell right now, in body or in spirit. Let yourself feel a little of what they carry, the way a parent feels a child's fever, just enough to know it's real. Then, on each out-breath, wish them ease.

wordCard.voice: I'm sick because the world is sick. Vimalakirti's answer: his illness comes from great compassion, like a parent sick beside a sick child. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: great compassion, which Vimalakirti names as the source of his sickness.

carryVoice: Your line: because the world is sick. Love that stays close feels the fever too. Until tomorrow.
